items.name: p05
items.direction: Narrate this as a popular, witty long-form history YouTube documentary about India. The Narrator is a deep, warm, confident storyteller: relaxed and conversational, curious, lightly funny, with a short comic pause before each punchline and before chapter turns. Chars voices the people in short dramatised scenes (merchants, engineers, scholars, servants, kings, emperors, sultans, officials, soldiers): short, punchy, expressive, following the bracketed style tags. Pronounce Indian names and places naturally, the way an Indian speaker would. VOICE IDENTITY (most important): the Narrator is always the same person: a low, warm baritone documentary host. Keep his voice identity and natural speaking pitch the same from the first line to the last, so it never sounds like a different or younger narrator. Emotion is welcome: show it freely through emphasis, energy, pace, louder and softer moments and dramatic pauses, as a real storyteller would. Never whisper or go breathy. PRONUNCIATION (say these names exactly like this, stress on the capital syllables): Aryabhata = AHR-yuh-BUH-tuh; Chaturanga = chuh-too-RUNG-uh; Nalanda = naa-LUN-daa.
lines: Around two thousand years ago, ships sailed from Egypt to India's southern coast, riding the monsoon winds. They went home loaded with pepper, gems and cotton cloth.

And Rome paid in gold. So much gold that the Roman writer Pliny complained about it. He grumbled that India drained the empire of fifty million sesterces every single year. Hoards of Roman coins still turn up in south India today.
Keep Pliny's complaint in mind. Seventeen centuries later, someone in India is going to make exactly the same complaint... the other way round.

In the north, newcomers from Central Asia, the Kushans, built an empire, and their greatest king became a champion of Buddhism. Remember our question? They came as outsiders. They stayed, and became part of India.
Then, around three twenty CE, a new family united the north: the Guptas. And what people remember about the Gupta age isn't its battles. It's its ideas.
In four ninety-nine, a twenty-three-year-old mathematician named Aryabhata wrote that the Earth spins on its own axis. That's about a thousand years before Copernicus.
So the sky turns around the Earth every night?
No. The Earth turns. The sky stays still.
Then why am I not dizzy?
[patiently] I'll explain tomorrow. If the Earth is still here.
Aryabhata also worked out pi to four decimal places: three point one four one six.

And Indian mathematicians were building the number system you use every single day: nine digits, plus a sign for nothing. A little later, another mathematician wrote down the rules for zero as a number in its own right.
Those numerals travelled to the Arab world, and then to Europe. Which is why Europeans called them... Arabic numerals. The numbers on your phone are Indian.

This age gave the world something else too: a war game on an eight-by-eight board, with elephants, chariots, horses and foot soldiers. Chaturanga. Carried west through Persia, it became the game we call chess.

Students crossed Asia to study at Nalanda, one of the world's first great universities. And in Delhi stands an iron pillar from this age that has stood in the rain for about sixteen hundred years... and has barely rusted.
In the far south, the Chola kings later built one of the greatest navies in Asian history, and sent it across the sea to attack kingdoms in Sumatra and Malaya.
This was the land Indians still call, in its richest times, Sone ki Chidiya: the Golden Bird.
And a bird that shiny gets noticed. In Afghanistan, a powerful sultan had just learned exactly how much gold was sitting inside India's temples.

lines: His name was Shah Jahan. And under him, the Mughal Empire reached the peak of its wealth and its show.

He sat on the Peacock Throne, made of gold and covered in jewels. And set into it was a diamond the size of a small egg: the Koh-i-Noor, the "Mountain of Light". Remember the diamond from the beginning? This is where its journey starts.

In this age, India was one of the richest places on Earth. And the secret wasn't diamonds. It was cloth. Remember the cotton from the Indus? Indian cotton now dressed people from Japan to Africa to London. Silver poured in from Europe and the Americas to pay for it.
When Shah Jahan's favourite wife, Mumtaz Mahal, died giving birth to their fourteenth child, he built her a tomb on the river at Agra.
Around twenty thousand workers and craftsmen. More than twenty years. White marble from Rajasthan, inlaid with stones from across Asia. The Taj Mahal.

Now, let's bust a myth. You've probably heard that once it was finished, Shah Jahan cut off the builders' hands, so they could never build anything as beautiful again. There's no evidence for it. No record from the time mentions it. It's a much later legend.
But Shah Jahan's ending was dark enough without it. His four sons fought a brutal war for the throne. The winner was Aurangzeb.
Aurangzeb had his brothers killed, and locked his own father inside the fort at Agra. From its windows, Shah Jahan could see the Taj across the river.
[not turning] Is my son coming to visit?
[quietly] Regards. I gave him an empire.
Aurangzeb ruled for nearly fifty years, and pushed the empire to its largest size ever. But he spent his last twenty-five years at war in the south, and he brought back the jizya tax.

His toughest enemy was a young Maratha leader from the hills near Pune: Shivaji, a master of fast raids and hill forts. Placed under house arrest in Agra, he escaped, as the famous story goes, hidden inside giant baskets of sweets.
After Aurangzeb died in seventeen oh seven, the empire cracked. Governors became kings. The Marathas spread across the centre of India.
And in seventeen thirty-nine, the Persian ruler Nadir Shah marched in and sacked Delhi. He carried home the Peacock Throne... and the Koh-i-Noor.
Remember Mahmud's camels? India's treasure was leaving again. But the next visitors weren't interested in thrones. They didn't come with armies. They came with account books.

lines: The young republic had a rough start. It lost a border war with China in nineteen sixty-two, and fought Pakistan in nineteen sixty-five. By the mid-sixties, India was so short of food that it depended on grain shipments from America.
Then came the Green Revolution: new high-yield wheat and rice, irrigation and fertiliser. Within about a decade, India could feed itself.
In nineteen seventy-one, India backed the independence struggle in East Pakistan and won a short war. A new country was born: Bangladesh.

In nineteen seventy-five, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi declared an Emergency. Elections were suspended, opponents jailed, newspapers censored. And when she finally called elections, the voters, the same voters of the picture symbols, threw her out.
For most of these years, India's economy was tightly controlled. You needed government permission to make almost anything. People called it the Licence Raj.
In nineteen ninety-one, it all came to a head. India nearly ran out of money. Its foreign reserves could pay for only about three weeks of imports.
To get an emergency loan, the government did something unthinkable. It flew forty-seven tonnes of its own gold to the Bank of England.
Remember Mahmud's camels, carrying India's gold away? Remember Naoroji's drain? Now India had to send its own gold to London.
Cargo: forty-seven tonnes of gold. Destination: London.
Wait... didn't the British take enough already?
This time, we're getting it back.

And they did. Because that crisis forced a revolution. A quiet economist named Manmohan Singh, the new finance minister, stood up in Parliament and quoted Victor Hugo: no power on Earth can stop an idea whose time has come.
India opened up. Lower taxes on imports. Private companies welcome. Foreign investment allowed. Growth took off, and software companies in Bengaluru and Hyderabad began serving the whole world.
In two thousand fourteen, India reached Mars on its very first try, for about seventy-four million dollars. Less than the Hollywood space film Gravity cost to make.
In two thousand twenty-three, Chandrayaan-3 became the first spacecraft to land near the Moon's south pole. That same year, India became the most populous country on Earth.
Narendra Modi has been Prime Minister since two thousand fourteen. Today India is the world's fifth-largest economy, and the IMF expects it to pass Japan next year.
To be fair, it still has a long way to go. Hundreds of millions still earn very little. Good jobs are scarce for the young. And critics worry about pressure on the press and on religious minorities.
But the Golden Bird is climbing again.
So think about everyone who came to take something from this land. Alexander. The Kushans. Mahmud. Ghori. Timur. Babur. Nadir Shah. A company from London.
Think about everything they carried off: gold on camels, a peacock throne, a diamond that now sits in the Tower of London, and a drain of wealth that ran for two hundred years.
And now, the question from the start. Why did almost every robber end up staying?
Here's the answer. India's wealth could always be carried away. India itself never could.

The Kushans became champions of Indian Buddhism. The sultans' soldiers gave India Urdu and qawwali. Babur arrived missing his melons, and his great-great-grandson built the Taj Mahal. Again and again, the invaders ended up eating India's food, speaking its languages, and building its monuments.
Only one never moved in. It ruled from an office in London, and it sent the money home. By the time it left, India's share of the world had fallen to about four percent.‡
Remember that sailor at Calicut, more than five hundred years ago? He came for spices, and for cloth so fine that Europe named it after the port where he stood.
Today, the world is coming back to buy from India again. Its software, its medicines, and yes, its cloth. India is once again one of the biggest cloth-makers on Earth.
The Golden Bird lost its gold more times than anyone can count. It never lost itself.
